GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from
Reasoning Teachers

Sahibzada Allahyar    Julia White    Dhruv Atreja    George Hurn-Maloney    Urchade Zaratiana Affiliation: Fastino Labs Email: {sahibzada,jwhite,dhruv,g,uz}@fastino.ai
Abstract

Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with GLiDE, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters.

Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens.

Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance–parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face Decision Index, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. GLiDE V1.2 (27B) ranks first on the Hugging Face Decision Index (edition 0.4.1, 22 October 2026) with a hidden-set score of 71.52, an expected calibration error of 2.0% and a median latency of 92.9 ms on a single GPU. It also shares first place on all three versions of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index (5, 8 and 15 November 2026). Both leaderboards are run by their maintainers, who evaluate every model themselves on test sets that model developers cannot see: fully hidden on Hugging Face, partly private on Artificial Analysis. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE 27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1%.

1 Introduction

Decision models and the reasoning gap.

Large language models are increasingly used not only to generate text, but also to make decisions: selecting tools, routing requests, classifying inputs, and choosing among predefined actions. In these settings, generating an answer token by token is often unnecessary. Decision models instead score candidate answers in a single forward pass, producing a probability distribution over the available choices. This approach has evolved from compact, schema-conditioned encoders such as GLiNER2 (Zaratiana et al., 2025) to larger systems including Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), Decider (Perplexity AI, 2026), and Mammoth (Kirkby et al., 2026). Yet a central tension remains: multi-step reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, while generating that reasoning introduces precisely the sequential computation that decision models seek to avoid. The challenge is therefore to capture the benefits of reasoning while retaining the speed of direct prediction, without sacrificing calibration or generalization (Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024; Recht et al., 2019).

Our approach.

We introduce GLiDE, a family of single-pass decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Starting from Qwen hybrid language models, we remove causal masking from their full-attention layers, allowing the context, question, and candidate answers to interact bidirectionally while retaining causal Gated DeltaNet layers (Figure 2). A dedicated readout then produces probabilities over the offered options. To transfer reasoning-informed supervision into this architecture, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a model evaluated after reasoning, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. In this way, GLiDE learns from the distributions produced by reasoning without generating intermediate reasoning at inference time.

Decision performance and calibration.

We first evaluate GLiDE on the Hugging Face Decision Index (Passos, 2026a), which ranks models using independently administered hidden test sets. On edition 0.4.1 (22 October 2026), GLiDE V1.2 (27B) achieves a score of 71.52, ranking first among 225 models and outperforming the runner-up by 1.77 points (Figure 4). It also leads on both hidden components, covering unseen questions from established skills and decisions in new domains. This performance is accompanied by an expected calibration error of 2.0% and a median latency of 92.9 ms on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, demonstrating that strong decision accuracy can coexist with reliable confidence estimates and efficient inference.

Hidden-set evaluation.

The Hugging Face Decision Index evaluates submitted models using private test sets administered by the benchmark maintainers. As of November 15, 2026, GLiDE models achieved competitive performance across multiple leaderboard revisions, with GLiDE 27B scoring 73.37 on the hidden evaluation sets. All five model sizes also lie on the reported performance–parameter Pareto frontier.

Scaling and recurrent depth.

Finally, we investigate how the approach extends across model sizes and inference-time computation budgets. We develop four smaller GLiDE models through progressive training and distillation from the 27B model. All five models lie on the performance–parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face Decision Index, each outperforming every evaluated alternative of equal or smaller size. We also investigate parameter-free recurrent depth, which increases computation by reapplying selected middle layers without introducing new weights or generating tokens. Combined with further checkpoint averaging, this produces GLiDE 27B, which reaches 73.37 on the Hugging Face Decision Index with an expected calibration error of 2.1%. Together, these results establish GLiDE as a family of fast, calibrated decision models that benefit from reasoning-informed training without requiring explicit reasoning generation at inference time.

Taken together, these findings show that strong, calibrated decision performance can be achieved across model scales without generating explicit reasoning at inference time. More broadly, GLiDE demonstrates how reasoning-informed supervision and additional computation within the model can improve decision quality while preserving the efficiency of direct candidate scoring.

2 Decision Model Architecture

Readers new to decision models may prefer to start with Appendix A, which builds the model from the base language model step by step.

2.1 Task Formulation

We consider decision-making tasks in which a model selects an answer from a finite set of candidates. A request consists of a context cc and MM questions:

ℛ=(c,{(qj,𝒜j)}j=1M),\mathcal{R}=\left(c,\{(q_{j},\mathcal{A}_{j})\}_{j=1}^{M}\right), (1)

where 𝒜j={aj,1,…,aj,Kj}\mathcal{A}_{j}=\{a_{j,1},\ldots,a_{j,K_{j}}\} denotes the candidate answers for question jj. For brevity, let uj=(c,qj,𝒜j)u_{j}=(c,q_{j},\mathcal{A}_{j}). The model predicts a categorical distribution:

pθ(⋅∣uj)∈ΔKj−1,∑k=1Kjpθ(k∣uj)=1.p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid u_{j})\in\Delta^{K_{j}-1},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^{K_{j}}p_{\theta}(k\mid u_{j})=1. (2)

The predicted decision and its confidence are

k^j\displaystyle\hat{k}_{j} =arg⁡maxk∈[Kj]​pθ​(k∣uj),\displaystyle=\arg\max_{k\in[K_{j}]}p_{\theta}(k\mid u_{j}), (3)
p^j\displaystyle\hat{p}_{j} =pθ​(k^j∣uj).\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\hat{k}_{j}\mid u_{j}).

Unlike autoregressive generation, decision inference requires a single forward pass, without generating intermediate reasoning or answer tokens. Appendix C formalizes typed outputs, cost-sensitive decisions, confidence-based deferral, and the semantics of batched questions.

2.2 Model Architecture

Figure 2 illustrates the architecture of GLiDE V1.2, from input encoding to single-pass decision probabilities.

Input encoding.

Each question is converted into a single sequence that concatenates the context, question, and candidate answers. The context appears once in each sequence, while each candidate is assigned a unique single-token code γk\gamma_{k}. A final answer prefix marks the position from which the model predicts the decision distribution. Formally, the input sequence is defined as

xj\displaystyle x_{j} =Tok⁡(c⊕qjCLOSE\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tok}(c\oplus q_{j} (4)
⊕⨁k=1Kj(γk⊕aj,k)⊕sans),\displaystyle\oplus\bigoplus_{k=1}^{K_{j}}(\gamma_{k}\oplus a_{j,k})\oplus s_{\mathrm{ans}}),

where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation and sanss_{\mathrm{ans}} is the final answer prefix. Questions from the same request are processed as separate sequences in one batch.

Hybrid decoder.

We build on Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), which contains 48 Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2025) and 16 full-attention layers. Standard causal attention is defined by

Attn⁡(Q,K,V,Ω)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤dk+Ω)​V,\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V;\Omega)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}+\Omega\right)V, (5)

with the causal mask

Ωi​j={0,j≤i,−∞,j>i.\Omega_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&j\leq i,\\ -\infty,&j>i.\end{cases} (6)

We remove this mask from the 16 full-attention layers, setting Ω=0\Omega=0. This allows bidirectional interaction between the context, question, and candidate answers. The Gated DeltaNet layers retain their causal recurrence and linear complexity in sequence length.

Option readout.

Let FθF_{\theta} denote the hybrid decoder and LjL_{j} the length of xjx_{j}. We extract the final hidden state at the answer prefix:

Hj=Fθ​(xj),hj=Hj​[Lj]∈ℝd.H_{j}=F_{\theta}(x_{j}),\qquad h_{j}=H_{j}[L_{j}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (7)

A dedicated linear readout maps this representation to logits over 255 possible option codes:

zj=W​hj,W∈ℝ255×d.z_{j}=Wh_{j},\qquad W\in\mathbb{R}^{255\times d}. (8)

Since each question may have a different number of candidate answers, we restrict the readout to the KjK_{j} option codes present in the input, discarding logits associated with unused codes. A softmax over the remaining logits then produces a normalized probability distribution over the offered candidates:

pθ​(k∣uj)=exp⁡(zj,k)∑ℓ=1Kjexp⁡(zj,ℓ)p_{\theta}(k\mid u_{j})=\frac{\exp(z_{j,k})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K_{j}}\exp(z_{j,\ell})} (9)

for k∈[Kj]k\in[K_{j}]. The readout is initialized from the corresponding rows of the pretrained language-model head. Thus, a single evaluation of FθF_{\theta} produces a normalized distribution over all offered answers, without autoregressive decoding.

3 Training

We train GLiDE V1.2 through progressive post-training, transferring reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference and refining them with diverse decision data and multi-teacher supervision. Figure 9 illustrates the evolution of the model across stages.

3.1 Progressive Training and Distillation

We train GLiDE through four successive stages, each building on the checkpoint produced by the preceding stage. The procedure first develops a reasoning-capable teacher, then converts it into a single-pass decision model before progressively refining its predictions.

Stage 1: Reasoning teacher.

We first adapt Qwen3.8-27B using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) in two steps. We begin by generating reasoning traces for training questions and retaining approximately 6,400 examples whose reasoning leads to the correct answer. Rank-64 LoRA adapters are trained on these examples with the base weights frozen, using next-token prediction on the reasoning traces and cross-entropy on the final answers. Next, the adapted model reasons over approximately 135K additional questions, and we collect its post-thinking probability distributions over the candidate answers. A second LoRA round trains the model to predict these distributions directly, without producing written reasoning. The resulting teacher can operate with or without explicit reasoning, providing both direct and post-thinking predictions for subsequent distillation. This is the only stage that uses LoRA.

Stage 2: Single-pass conversion.

Starting from the reasoning teacher, we remove causal masking from the full-attention layers and introduce the dedicated option readout. We then distill soft probability distributions from multiple teachers, including the reasoning model’s post-thinking predictions, to train the architecture for direct decision scoring in a single forward pass.

Stage 3: Short training rounds.

We then continue training through five short rounds. After each round, the updated checkpoint is averaged equally with its parent, yielding GLiDE V1.1. This recursive averaging gives the latest update half of the final weight, the preceding update one quarter, and progressively smaller contributions to earlier rounds, helping retain previously learned capabilities while incorporating new refinements.

Stage 4: Final post-training.

Finally, we continue training GLiDE V1.1 on a rebuilt mixture of diverse decision tasks, using task-specific multi-teacher distributions as supervision. This stage consolidates the preceding improvements and produces GLiDE V1.2, our final decision model.

Distilling reasoning.

The central challenge is to preserve the benefits of slow, multi-step reasoning without performing it at inference time. For input xx, let qthinkq_{\mathrm{think}} and qdirectq_{\mathrm{direct}} denote the reasoning teacher’s answer distributions with and without thinking, respectively. We construct the target distribution as

q={12​(qthink+qdirect),κ⁡(x)<η,qdirect,κ⁡(x)≥η,q=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}(q_{\mathrm{think}}+q_{\mathrm{direct}}),&\kappa(x)<\eta,\\ q_{\mathrm{direct}},&\kappa(x)\geq\eta,\end{cases} (10)

where κ⁡(x)=maxk⁡qdirect​(k∣x)\kappa(x)=\max_{k}q_{\mathrm{direct}}(k\mid x) is the direct model’s confidence and η=0.8\eta=0.8. In words: if the teacher is already at least 80% confident without thinking, we use its direct distribution. Otherwise, we average its direct and post-thinking distributions. Averaging the distributions retains the direct model’s signal while incorporating changes induced by reasoning. This provides post-thinking supervision primarily when the direct model is uncertain. Given a gold answer yy and teacher distribution qq, the student minimizes

ℒ⁡(θ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\theta)={} −α​log⁡pθ​(y∣x)\displaystyle-\alpha\log p_{\theta}(y\mid x) (11)
+(1−α)DKL(q∥pθ),\displaystyle+(1-\alpha)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_{\theta}),

with α=0.3\alpha=0.3. The first term rewards the correct answer. The second makes the student match the teacher’s full distribution. Soft targets convey not only the preferred answer but also the uncertainty remaining after reasoning, allowing the student to approximate the teacher’s decision distribution in a single pass.

3.2 Training Data and Generation

GLiDE is trained on a mixture of existing datasets and generated decision examples spanning classification, extraction, knowledge, reasoning, tool use, and safety. We use procedural generation and language-model-based annotation to expand task coverage and introduce variation in question structure, candidate answers, and difficulty. The final post-training stage contains 374,720 examples. Across the training pipeline, we use more than 1.6 million distinct questions from over 500 task families, corresponding to approximately 2.3 billion training tokens. Table 2 summarizes the scale of the training data..

3.3 Multi-Teacher Supervision

The final training stage combines complementary teachers, including existing single-pass decision models, an earlier checkpoint of our model, and an annotator. Since teacher performance differs across tasks, we use task-specific log-linear pooling (Genest and Zidek, 1986). For task family ff, the aggregated target is

qf​(k∣x)=exp⁡(sf,k​(x))∑ℓ=1Kxexp⁡(sf,ℓ​(x)),q_{f}(k\mid x)=\frac{\exp(s_{f,k}(x))}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K_{x}}\exp(s_{f,\ell}(x))}, (12)

where

sf,k​(x)=∑t=1Tλf,t​log⁡pt​(k∣x).s_{f,k}(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lambda_{f,t}\log p_{t}(k\mid x). (13)

Here ptp_{t} denotes teacher tt and λf,t∈[0,4]\lambda_{f,t}\in[0,4] its task-specific weight. We optimize these weights by minimizing gold-label negative log-likelihood on a held-out 5% slice of the training data, using two-fold cross-fitting.

Gold anchoring.

To limit propagation of teacher errors, pooled targets are subject to gold-consistency checks and replaced by gold-anchored targets when necessary. The downstream student gain from this procedure remains within single-seed variability.

Abstention.

For knowledge tasks, “I don’t know” is treated as an ordinary candidate answer. Rather than imitating teacher uncertainty, we derive abstention targets from the starting student’s confidence, encouraging it to abstain when its own knowledge is insufficient.

3.4 Optimization Details

The final stage uses full-parameter fine-tuning with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, batch size 128, and 2,928 steps over one epoch. Candidate options are shuffled during training to reduce position bias. Each seed requires approximately six hours on eight B200 GPUs. The released model averages the weights of two independently trained seeds  (Wortsman et al., 2022).

4 Experimental Setup

We evaluate GLiDE V1.2 on decision-making benchmarks covering accuracy, generalization, calibration, and inference efficiency. Our primary evaluation is the Hugging Face Decision Index, complemented by externally administered benchmarks and held-out internal evaluation sets.

4.1 Benchmarks

Decision Index.

The Decision Index (Passos, 2026a) evaluates decision models across 37 public benchmarks spanning five task categories. Since October 20, 2026, its official ranking has relied exclusively on two hidden evaluation sets administered by the benchmark maintainers: (i) same-skill, measuring generalization to unseen questions from known task families, and (ii) new-domain, evaluating decisions in domains absent from the public benchmarks. Let SS and OO denote the normalized scores on the two hidden sets. The overall ranking score is Full=0.6​S+0.4​O\mathrm{Full}=0.6S+0.4O. Models must complete inference without intermediate reasoning and satisfy a one-second latency limit on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU. We report results from edition 0.4.1 (October 22, 2026).

Artificial Analysis Decision Index.

We also evaluate GLiDE on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index (Artificial Analysis, 2026a), an externally administered benchmark assessing decision-making capabilities across knowledge, reasoning, tool use, and safety. Artificial Analysis evaluates models through their public APIs using a standardized protocol and publishes the resulting scores independently of model developers. The original version combines four equally weighted evaluations: AA-Omniscience-Decision, which measures knowledge reliability and selective answering (Jackson et al., 2025); multiple-choice questions from Humanity’s Last Exam (Center for AI Safety et al., 2026); When2Call, which evaluates tool-use decisions (Ross et al., 2025); and WildGuardTest, which assesses safety classification (Han et al., 2024). We report the official scores published by Artificial Analysis. The index has been revised twice since. Version 2 (8 November 2026; Artificial Analysis, 2026b) uses six evaluations. It adds decisions about documents and a test of whether a decision stays the same when the question is reworded, and it draws 45% of its weight from private data, up from 25%. Version 2.1 followed within days. It revised the consistency test and rescored every model. We report all three versions.

Hidden test sets.

The Hugging Face ranking uses only hidden questions. The Artificial Analysis index combines a private set with public ones. We have never had access to the hidden questions, their answers, or per-question results of either benchmark; we see only the aggregate scores published by their maintainers.

Complementary evaluations.

To assess performance beyond the primary leaderboard, we also evaluate on JevBench, SciFact, a held-out clinical decision set, and an internal regression suite spanning eight real-world decision categories.

4.2 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate three complementary properties of decision models: predictive accuracy, calibration, and inference efficiency.

Decision performance.

We report the official benchmark scores and the two hidden components SS and OO. For the Decision Index, public benchmarks are scored using chance-corrected skill and do not contribute to the official ranking.

Calibration.

We measure expected calibration error (ECE), which compares predicted confidence with empirical accuracy across BB confidence bins:

ECE=∑b=1BnbN​|acc⁡(b)−conf⁡(b)|,\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{n_{b}}{N}\left|\mathrm{acc}(b)-\mathrm{conf}(b)\right|, (14)

where nbn_{b} is the number of predictions in bin bb. Lower ECE indicates better calibration.

Inference efficiency.

We report median inference latency on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, following the leaderboard protocol. All decisions are produced in one forward pass, without autoregressive decoding.

4.3 Development Evaluation

We evaluate candidate checkpoints on internal development sets covering accuracy on held-out task families and domains, input robustness, and regression checks. Final benchmark scores are obtained through evaluations administered by the benchmark maintainers. Appendix E provides additional methodological context.

5 Results

We evaluate GLiDE V1.2 in terms of decision accuracy, generalization, calibration, and inference efficiency. We further examine the contributions of non-causal attention and soft-target distillation. Each paragraph below opens with the question it answers.

5.1 Main Results

Decision performance.

Does GLiDE V1.2 decide better than other models on questions it has never seen? Table 1 reports results on the Hugging Face Decision Index (edition 0.4.1, 22 October 2026). GLiDE V1.2 achieves a Full score of 71.52, ranking first of 225 models, 1.77 points ahead of Jeffan-31B; this margin is about twice the board’s 0.9-point tie margin, while six models share third place within 0.9 points of one another. GLiDE V1.2 is also first on each hidden component: 68.31 on same-skill (next best 65.98) and 76.32 on new-domain (next best 75.58). Figure 4 shows that this lead does not come at the cost of calibration or speed. Every model with better calibration scores at most 61.3, and every faster model scores at most 68.0. A comparison with Drex Max (Dhankhar et al., 2026) helps isolate the effect of training. Drex Max starts from the same Qwen3.8-27B base and makes the same two architectural changes: non-causal attention and a 255-way readout. It scores 66.60 on this board, 4.92 points below GLiDE V1.2. The two models share a backbone and readout but differ in how they were trained.

Generalization.

Does the model do as well on hidden questions as on public ones? GLiDE V1.2’s Full score is 0.47 points below its public score. Across the 225 models, Full scores track public ones (slope 0.98, Spearman ρ=0.95\rho=0.95) but sit about 4 points lower; a model with GLiDE V1.2’s public score is expected to reach 67.3, and GLiDE V1.2’s 71.52 lies inside the 95% prediction interval [55.0, 79.5] of a fit that excludes it. The small gap is consistent with good generalization, although a single benchmark cannot establish distribution-wide robustness.

Artificial Analysis evaluation.

We additionally evaluate the frozen GLiDE V1.2 checkpoint on three successive versions of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, administered through the model’s public API. Across these versions, GLiDE remains within 0.6 points of the highest unrounded score. The subsequent revisions introduce new tasks and provide complementary evidence of performance stability under changes to the benchmark. Table 5 reports the results, and Appendix F lists all evaluated models.

5.2 Calibration and Efficiency

Probability calibration.

When the model says it is 90% sure, is it right about 90% of the time? GLiDE V1.2 has an expected calibration error of 2.0% (10 bins on the board’s sample; interval about [1.7, 2.4]), the lowest among the ten highest-ranked models (Table 7). Its mean confidence exceeds its accuracy by 1.1 points (82.6% vs. 81.5%), whereas the other nine are overconfident by 2.5 to 10.5 points. The 56% of its answers given with confidence above 0.9 are correct 97.4% of the time. Its Brier score, which mixes calibration and accuracy, is slightly higher than those of three models that are 0.9–1.3 points more accurate on this sample. We apply no correction after training, such as a fitted temperature. The probabilities are the plain softmax of the readout, so the calibration is a result of training and not of a later fix. Calibration differs by task area: ECE is 1.8% on language tasks, 3.5% on retrieval, 3.9% on tools, 4.2% on arts and 7.5% on knowledge. Figure 4c plots confidence against accuracy.

Acting only on confident answers.

If an application acts only when the model is confident, how accurate are those answers? Table 6 answers this on the same sample. Accepting every answer gives 81.5% accuracy. Accepting only answers with a confidence of at least 0.8 keeps 68% of them, and 95.0% of those are correct. At 0.9, 56% are kept and 97.4% are correct. An application can therefore trade coverage for accuracy by setting a threshold, with no retraining (Appendix C).

Inference latency.

How fast is the model? GLiDE V1.2 has a median latency of 92.9 ms on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, 1.3×1.3\times faster than Jeffan-31B, 2.4×2.4\times faster than mammoth-1 and 2.1×2.1\times faster than d3-turbo v1.1; every faster model on the board scores at least 3.5 points lower. Figure 4b shows score against latency for all models.

Complementary evaluations.

How does the model perform on additional task sets? GLiDE V1.2 is best on three of four complementary benchmarks in Table 4; on JevBench it trails the best open model by 0.87 points.

5.3 Ablation Study

Which part of the single-pass conversion helps: removing the causal mask, training on soft targets, or both? Table 3 changes one thing per row. The first row is the Stage 1 model before any conversion training. The second keeps the causal mask and trains on gold labels. The third removes the mask. The fourth replaces gold labels with soft targets. The last also re-formats 30% of the examples. The table reports a composite development score, held-out accuracy, and sensitivity to input-format perturbations.

Table 3 compares single-pass conversion variants trained on the same 125K examples with one seed. Removing the causal mask raises the development score from 60.42 to 61.78 and reduces format sensitivity from 1.25 to 0.22 points; adding soft targets raises the development score to 62.59 and held-out accuracy to 89.16%. All three measures move in the same direction, but each step is within single-seed variability, so we treat these results as indicative rather than conclusive. Format augmentation did not help and was not retained.

6 Recurrent Depth and Model Scaling

We investigate two extensions of GLiDE V1.2: increasing inference-time computation without introducing additional parameters, and transferring the training procedure to smaller model scales. Figure 5 summarizes the resulting model lineage. Unless stated otherwise, development uses internal evaluation data and reported comparisons use separate held-out sets. Hugging Face Decision Index scores are externally administered measurements from edition 0.4.1  (Passos, 2026b).

6.1 GLiDE 27B

Parameter averaging.

We train two additional checkpoints from the same lineage on broader mixtures of approximately 1.7 million questions each. Individually, they change held-out performance by +0.21+0.21 and −0.20-0.20 points and do not satisfy the predefined improvement threshold of +0.5+0.5. We then form a convex parameter average assigning weight 1/21/2 to GLiDE V1.2 and 1/41/4 to each additional checkpoint. The averaged model improves held-out performance by 0.860.86 points. This result is consistent with prior observations that checkpoints from a shared fine-tuning lineage can remain connected in weight space (Wortsman et al., 2022; Izmailov et al., 2018). Across the complete lineage, training uses approximately 3.9 billion tokens from 3.4 million distinct questions.

Parameter-free recurrent depth.

GLiDE 27B uses the parameters of the averaged model without further training. At inference time, two middle blocks—layers 24–35 and 36–47 of the 64-layer network—are each applied twice. For a block map FF, the recurrent update is

xk+1=xk+η[F(xk)−xk],k=0,1,η=12,x_{k+1}=x_{k}+\eta\,[F(x_{k})-x_{k}],\;\;k=0,1,\;\;\eta=\tfrac{1}{2}, (15)

where x0x_{0} is the block input and x2x_{2} is passed to the subsequent layer. Equation 15 defines a damped fixed-point iteration related to weight-tied and recurrent-depth networks (Dehghani et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025). It adds computation but no trainable parameters. The damping coefficient limits the distribution shift presented to downstream layers; in our experiments, the undamped update (η=1\eta=1) performs worse. Figure 6 illustrates the procedure.

Evaluation protocol.

Candidate configurations vary the repeated layer blocks, recurrence count, and damping schedule. Configuration choice uses internal development data. We compare the selected configuration with the averaged-model baseline on two separate held-out sets.

Results.

Recurrent depth improves the two held-out scores by 0.690.69 points (interval [0.02,1.42][0.02,1.42]) and 0.560.56 points ([0.27,0.89][0.27,0.89]), respectively. GLiDE 27B obtains a hidden-set score of 73.37, compared with 71.52 for GLiDE V1.2; this difference includes both parameter averaging and recurrent depth. Median latency increases from 92.9 to 122 ms because 24 of the 64 layers are evaluated twice. Calibration remains similar, with ECE increasing from 2.0% to 2.1%. On the benchmark calibration sample, 58% of predictions have confidence above 0.9, of which 97.3% are correct.

Ablations.

Applying each block three times performs worse than applying it twice, and introducing trainable loop parameters does not improve over the parameter-free update. High-learning-rate distillation and alternative parameter averages also fail to improve held-out performance.

6.2 Scaling Across Model Sizes

Training procedure.

We construct four smaller variants: GLiDE 9B, 2B, 0.8B, and 0.4B. The 9B, 2B, and 0.8B variants use base models with the same hybrid architecture and tokenizer as Qwen3.8-27B, allowing the examples and option labels from Section 3 to transfer directly. A final distillation epoch trains each model to match the complete output distribution of GLiDE 27B over 3.4 million questions. This step improves held-out performance by 2.4 points at 0.8B parameters and 1.1 points at 2B parameters. GLiDE 9B additionally uses low-learning-rate distillation, parameter averaging, and recurrent depth. GLiDE 0.4B uses a bidirectional encoder trained against the same 27B output distributions. Generating labels for the 3.4 million-question corpus required 4.5 hours on 22 GPUs.

Data screening.

Before training, later data underwent repeated near-duplicate screening using n-gram overlap, MinHash similarity, and item-level rules. Matching questions were dropped and not replaced. Appendix E.2 describes the corresponding controls for the final-stage mixture.

Scaling results.

Table 8 and Figure 8 report the externally administered measurements. All five GLiDE models lie on the score--parameter Pareto frontier and exceed every evaluated alternative of equal or smaller size by 3.2 to 10.9 points. Median latency ranges from 18 to 122 ms. GLiDE 27B has the second-highest score among 300 models, while GLiDE 9B is the smallest listed model that exceeds the Jev 1.14 reference score. The public weights for all five models are available online.11 1 https://huggingface.co/fastino

7 Conclusion

We introduced GLiDE V1.2, a decision model that distills reasoning into a single forward pass. By combining non-causal full attention, a dedicated option readout, and multi-teacher distillation, the model produces calibrated probabilities over candidate decisions without generating intermediate reasoning. On the Hugging Face Decision Index (edition 0.4.1, 22 October 2026), GLiDE V1.2 achieves a score of 71.52, ranking first among 225 models and leading on both hidden evaluation sets, with an expected calibration error of 2.0% and a median latency of 92.9 ms. These results extend beyond the initial model. Without retraining, GLiDE V1.2 remains within 0.6 points of the highest score across three versions of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE 27B, which reaches 73.37 without introducing additional parameters. Across five model sizes spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters, each GLiDE model outperforms all evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. Together, these findings demonstrate that reasoning-informed training can enable strong, calibrated decision-making across model scales while preserving the efficiency of direct inference.

Appendix A From a language model to a decision model, step by step

This appendix explains in plain terms how GLiDE V1.2 is built from its base language model. It assumes only a basic knowledge of transformers. Sections 2 and 3 give the formal version, and Table 9 summarizes the changes.

A.1 The starting point

Qwen3.8-27B is an ordinary language model: it reads a sequence of tokens and predicts the next one. It has 64 layers and a hidden size of 5,120, and its last layer gives a score to each of about 248,000 vocabulary tokens. The layers are of two kinds.

  • •

    16 self-attention layers. In each, every token looks back at the earlier tokens and combines what it finds.

  • •

    48 Gated DeltaNet layers. Each reads the sequence from left to right and carries a running summary, much like a recurrent network. Its cost grows linearly with the length of the input, which keeps long documents cheap.

Both kinds are causal: a token can use only what comes before it. A model that writes text one token at a time needs this, because the later tokens do not exist yet.

A.2 The goal

A decision model answers a different kind of request. It receives a context, a question and a list of options, and returns one probability per option. For example:

Context: Order 1182. The parcel arrived damaged; two photos attached.
Question: What should the agent do next?
Options: (A) refund (B) replace (C) escalate (D) ask for more information
Wanted output: A 0.64, B 0.21, C 0.11, D 0.04

A language model could answer this by writing text, but that has three drawbacks. Writing is slow, because every generated token needs another pass through the network. The text has to be parsed. And the probabilities of the options are not given directly. Letting the model reason step by step before it answers improves accuracy, but multiplies the cost.

We want the accuracy of the reasoning model at the cost of a single pass. The six steps below get there.

A.3 Step 1: write the request as one prompt

The context, the question and the options are placed in a single prompt. Each option is given a one-token code (A, B, C, …). The prompt ends with the prefix “Answer: (”, so that the next token a language model would write is the code of its answer.

A.4 Step 2: read the answer from one position

The network turns the prompt into one vector per token. We keep only the vector at the last token, hh, which has 5,120 numbers. A small matrix WW with 255 rows, one for each possible option code, turns hh into 255 scores, z=W​hz=Wh. We keep the scores of the options that were actually offered (four in the example) and apply a softmax. The result is one probability per option, and the probabilities sum to one.

This readout replaces the original output layer, which scored 248,000 tokens. WW does not start from random values: each row is copied from the original output layer’s row for the same code token. So before any training, the readout scores option A exactly as the language model scored the token A.

There are 255 rows because we use 255 single-token codes: the 26 letters, then two-letter codes. A question can therefore have at most 255 options.

A.5 Step 3: let every token see the whole prompt

In a language model, the attention mask lets token ii attend only to tokens 1,…,i1,\ldots,i. For a decision, this restriction is unnecessary, because the whole prompt is known before the model starts. It is also harmful: the context is read before the question has been seen, and option A is read before options B, C and D.

We remove the mask in the 16 self-attention layers. Every token can then attend to every other token. The model can read the context knowing the question, and it can compare the options with each other. We leave the 48 Gated DeltaNet layers unchanged. They are recurrent by design, and leaving them alone keeps their linear cost.

Two consequences follow. First, the model can no longer write text, because writing depends on the mask. Second, the pretrained weights have never seen “future” tokens, so the model has to be trained before it can use them. That is the job of the next step.

A.6 Step 4: train on probabilities, not only on answers

Each training example consists of a prompt, the correct option, and a target distribution over the options, supplied by one or more teacher models. The loss (Equation 11) adds two terms: 0.3 times the cross-entropy with the correct option, and 0.7 times the KL divergence from the target distribution.

The second term is what separates this from ordinary classification training. A label says only that A is right. A target such as (0.70, 0.05, 0.25, 0.00)(0.70,\,0.05,\,0.25,\,0.00) also says that C is a plausible alternative and that D is not. A student trained on such targets learns how sure to be, not only what to answer. This is where the model’s calibration comes from. No temperature or other correction is fitted after training.

A.7 Step 5: move the thinking into training

One teacher is a version of the base model itself that reasons before it answers (Stage 1 in Section 3). For each training question we let this teacher write out its reasoning, and then record the probability it gives to each option. The student never sees the reasoning text. It sees only the distribution that the teacher reached after thinking, and learns to produce that distribution directly.

The cost of thinking is therefore paid once, during training, and not on every request. Thinking does not help on every question. If the teacher is already confident without reasoning, we use its direct distribution. Otherwise, we average its direct and post-thinking distributions (Equation 10).

A.8 Step 6: refine in rounds and average the weights

After the conversion, five short training rounds follow. After every round, we average the new weights with the weights the round started from. This keeps what earlier rounds learned. A final stage retrains the model on a rebuilt data mixture, with targets pooled from several teachers (Section 3). The released model is the average of two such runs with different random seeds.

A.9 What comes out

The finished model takes a prompt and returns one probability per option, in a single pass that takes a median of 92.9 ms. An application can take the most probable option. It can also act only when that probability is high enough, and pass the other cases to a person (Appendix C).

A.10 After GLiDE V1.2

Three later steps build on the finished model (Section 6). None changes the picture above: the model still returns one probability per option in a single pass.

  • •

    Average in two more models. Two further models were trained on broader data. Their weights were averaged with those of GLiDE V1.2.

  • •

    Run some layers twice. GLiDE 27B applies two blocks of middle layers twice at inference, moving half-way each time. The model computes more per question with no new weights and no generated tokens.

  • •

    Teach smaller models. Smaller models of the same design repeat the recipe. They are then trained to match the output distributions of the 27B model.

Appendix B Related Work

Distillation and one-pass reasoning.

Knowledge distillation transfers a teacher’s soft distribution to a student (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim and Rush, 2016), including information in the probability mass assigned to incorrect answers (Menon et al., 2021). Prior work has compressed chain-of-thought reasoning through sampled rationales, final answers, removed reasoning steps, or latent tokens (Hsieh et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024; Goyal et al., 2024). In contrast, we distill the complete post-thinking answer distribution, preserving the teacher’s residual uncertainty.

Single-pass decision models.

Schema-conditioned encoders such as GLiNER, GLiNER2, and GLiGuard support efficient prediction over natural-language labels or schemas (Zaratiana et al., 2024; Zaratiana et al., 2025; Zaratiana et al., 2026a; Zaratiana et al., 2026b). Work on non-causal decoders removes causal masks to produce strong representations (BehnamGhader et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2025); in our hybrid decoder, we unmask only the full-attention layers. Because option-symbol scoring can introduce order bias (Robinson et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024), we use a dedicated readout and shuffle options during training. Drex Max (Dhankhar et al., 2026), developed concurrently, uses the same backbone, also removes the causal mask, and also adds a 255-way readout. Its training differs: it adds consistency losses and a reinforcement-learning stage.

Calibration and abstention.

Neural networks and language models are often overconfident (Guo et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024). Selective prediction therefore adds a reject mechanism (Chow, 1970; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Kamath et al., 2020); we train explicit abstention as an ordinary option and expose probabilities for application-level deferral.

Appendix C Decision-model output semantics

Section 2 defines how GLiDE V1.2 maps a context, question, and finite answer set to a categorical distribution. This appendix specifies how that distribution is interpreted by an application. It also makes explicit several operational properties that are separate from the network architecture: typed questions, cost-sensitive decisions, deferral, permutation equivariance, and the independence of batched questions.

C.1 Typed questions

For question jj, let

pj=(pj,1,…,pj,Kj)∈ΔKj−1p_{j}=(p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,K_{j}})\in\Delta^{K_{j}-1}

be the distribution from Equation 9. The same distribution supports three output types.

Choice.

For an unordered set of named actions, the default decision and its confidence are

k^j=arg⁡maxk∈[Kj]⁡pj,k,p^j=pj,k^j.\hat{k}_{j}=\arg\max_{k\in[K_{j}]}p_{j,k},\qquad\hat{p}_{j}=p_{j,\hat{k}_{j}}.

The option descriptions are part of the input, so the actions need not belong to a fixed global label vocabulary. The model can score at most 255 options because its readout contains 255 single-token option codes.

Yes/no.

If the two options are “yes” and “no”, the useful scalar is

sj=pj​(yes),pj​(no)=1−sj.s_{j}=p_{j}(\mathrm{yes}),\qquad p_{j}(\mathrm{no})=1-s_{j}.

A threshold of 1/21/2 is optimal only when false positives and false negatives have equal cost. If their costs are respectively CFPC_{\mathrm{FP}} and CFNC_{\mathrm{FN}}, the minimum-expected-cost rule predicts yes when

sj≥CFPCFP+CFN.s_{j}\geq\frac{C_{\mathrm{FP}}}{C_{\mathrm{FP}}+C_{\mathrm{FN}}}.

Thus an application can change its operating point without retraining the model.

Ordered score.

Suppose the options represent ordered numerical levels v1<⋯<vKjv_{1}<\cdots<v_{K_{j}}. The modal and expected scores are

v^jmode=varg⁡maxk⁡pj,k,v^jmean=∑k=1Kjpj,k​vk.\hat{v}^{\,\mathrm{mode}}_{j}=v_{\arg\max_{k}p_{j,k}},\qquad\hat{v}^{\,\mathrm{mean}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{j}}p_{j,k}v_{k}.

The full distribution also exposes ambiguity through

Var⁡(vj)=∑k=1Kjpj,k​(vk−v^jmean)2.\operatorname{Var}(v_{j})=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{j}}p_{j,k}\left(v_{k}-\hat{v}^{\,\mathrm{mean}}_{j}\right)^{2}.

For example, (0.05,0.10,0.20,0.45,0.20)(0.05,0.10,0.20,0.45,0.20) over levels 0,…,40,\ldots,4 has mode 33, mean 2.652.65, and retains the information that adjacent levels remain plausible.

C.2 Automation, deferral, and abstention

The model distribution and the application’s decision policy are distinct. A common selective policy (Chow, 1970; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017) automates only sufficiently confident predictions:

δτ​(uj)={k^j,p^j≥τ,defer,p^j<τ.\delta_{\tau}(u_{j})=\begin{cases}\hat{k}_{j},&\hat{p}_{j}\geq\tau,\\ \mathrm{defer},&\hat{p}_{j}<\tau.\end{cases}

On an evaluation set of NN questions, this policy has coverage

Cov(τ)=1N∑j=1N𝟏[p^j≥τ]\operatorname{Cov}(\tau)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[\hat{p}_{j}\geq\tau]

and selective risk

Risk⁡(τ)=∑j𝟏[p^j≥τ]𝟏[k^j≠yj]∑j𝟏[p^j≥τ].\operatorname{Risk}(\tau)=\frac{\sum_{j}\mathbf{1}[\hat{p}_{j}\geq\tau]\mathbf{1}[\hat{k}_{j}\neq y_{j}]}{\sum_{j}\mathbf{1}[\hat{p}_{j}\geq\tau]}.

Increasing τ\tau usually lowers coverage and aims to lower risk; calibration determines whether confidence has a stable operational meaning on the deployment population. Deferral is not the same as explicit abstention. Deferral is imposed by the caller after inference and can use any threshold. Explicit abstention instead adds an “I don’t know” option ⊥\bot to the candidate set, so that

pj∈ΔKj,k^j∈{1,…,Kj,⊥}.p_{j}\in\Delta^{K_{j}},\qquad\hat{k}_{j}\in\{1,\ldots,K_{j},\bot\}.

It is therefore a behavior learned from training targets, not a post-hoc confidence rule. An application may combine both mechanisms: accept ⊥\bot when the model selects it, and defer any remaining answer below a chosen confidence threshold.

C.3 Batched questions and independence

A request may contain MM questions sharing a context cc. Each is rendered as its own sequence,

xj=Tok(c,qj,𝒜j),j=1,…,M,x_{j}=\operatorname{Tok}(c,q_{j},\mathcal{A}_{j}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,M,

and the sequences are padded and evaluated in one batch:

(p1,…,pM)=BatchEvalθ⁡(x1,…,xM).(p_{1},\ldots,p_{M})=\operatorname{BatchEval}_{\theta}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{M}).

Batching shares a device call but does not couple the answer distributions: the API exposes MM marginals rather than a joint distribution. If an application interprets them independently, the induced joint distribution is

p⁡(k^1,…,k^M∣ℛ)=∏j=1Mpj​(k^j∣c,qj,𝒜j).p(\hat{k}_{1},\ldots,\hat{k}_{M}\mid\mathcal{R})=\prod_{j=1}^{M}p_{j}(\hat{k}_{j}\mid c,q_{j},\mathcal{A}_{j}).

Consequently, cross-question constraints—for example, requiring exactly one of several flags to be true—must be enforced by a downstream constrained decoder or represented as one joint choice question. The context is included once within each question sequence, but is repeated across the MM batched sequences.

C.4 Option order and semantic equivariance

Candidate order should not change the underlying decision. For a permutation π\pi of the KjK_{j} options, the desired equivariance property is

pθ​(π⁡(k)∣c,qj,π⁡(𝒜j))=pθ​(k∣c,qj,𝒜j).p_{\theta}\!\left(\pi(k)\mid c,q_{j},\pi(\mathcal{A}_{j})\right)=p_{\theta}(k\mid c,q_{j},\mathcal{A}_{j}).

This property is not guaranteed by the architecture because each option is paired with an ordered code and occupies a different prompt position. Shuffling options during training, while applying the same permutation to the target distribution, encourages approximate equivariance. Keeping the full option descriptions in the prompt also makes the prediction depend on their semantics rather than on a fixed meaning for code A, B, and so on.

Appendix D The pipeline

Figure 9 gives the end-to-end lineage from the pretrained base model to the released checkpoint, including staged post-training and the construction of supervision from routed teachers.

D.1 Checkpoint lineage

Let θ0\theta_{0} denote the Qwen3.8-27B parameters. The four stages form a directed checkpoint lineage rather than four independent training runs:

θ1\displaystyle\theta_{1} =𝒯reason​(θ0,Dreason),\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{reason}}(\theta_{0};D_{\mathrm{reason}}), (16)
θ2\displaystyle\theta_{2} =𝒯convert​(θ1,Dconvert,Qteacher),\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{convert}}(\theta_{1};D_{\mathrm{convert}},Q_{\mathrm{teacher}}),
θ3\displaystyle\theta_{3} =𝒯rounds(5)​(θ2)=θV1​.1,\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{rounds}}^{(5)}(\theta_{2})=\theta_{\mathrm{V1.1}},
θ4,s\displaystyle\theta_{4,s} =𝒯final(θV1​.1;Dfinal,Qrouted,s),s∈{1,2}.\displaystyle=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{final}}(\theta_{\mathrm{V1.1}};D_{\mathrm{final}},Q_{\mathrm{routed}},s),s\in\{1,2\}.

Here 𝒯reason\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{reason}} produces the thinking-enabled teacher; 𝒯convert\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{convert}} introduces non-causal full attention and the 255-way option readout while distilling post-thinking behavior; and 𝒯rounds(5)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{rounds}}^{(5)} denotes five short training rounds. In round rr, the newly trained checkpoint θ~3,r\widetilde{\theta}_{3,r} is averaged with the parent that initialized it,

θ3,r=12(θ3,r−1+θ~3,r),r=1,…,5,\theta_{3,r}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\theta_{3,r-1}+\widetilde{\theta}_{3,r}\right),\qquad r=1,\ldots,5, (17)

which limits forgetting while accumulating the updates. Both final seeds start from the same GLiDE V1.1 checkpoint; they differ only through training stochasticity. The released parameters are their uniform average,

θV1​.2=12​(θ4,1+θ4,2).\theta_{\mathrm{V1.2}}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\theta_{4,1}+\theta_{4,2}\right). (18)

D.2 Supervision path

The final stage does not train directly on raw labels alone. Its 374,720 questions first pass through format normalization and data-quality screening. Each retained row ii contains an input xix_{i}, gold option yiy_{i}, task family fif_{i}, and routed soft target qiq_{i}. For ordinary rows, qiq_{i} is the cross-fitted, task-specific log-linear teacher pool of Equation 12; incorrect teacher consensus is replaced by a gold-anchored target. Knowledge rows instead use the starting student’s own correctness and confidence to decide whether the target should favor the answer or the explicit abstention option. At each optimization step, the candidate options, their codes, the gold index, and every coordinate of qiq_{i} are permuted together. The student then minimizes Equation 11. This ordering is important: teacher routing and gold anchoring define the target before option shuffling, while the shared permutation preserves its semantics and prevents a code position from becoming a label shortcut.

Appendix E Development Evaluation

Internal development evaluation covered held-out task families and domains, input robustness, abstention, and regression checks. A composite development score summarized these measurements for checkpoint comparison. Official hidden evaluations remained externally administered and returned only aggregate final-model results.

E.1 Statistical analysis

Unless stated otherwise, bracketed intervals compare two models on the same items using paired percentile bootstrap resampling within each skill. The ECE interval is a parametric bootstrap from the board’s confidence bins, and the regression interval in §5 is a tt prediction interval. Counts written with K or M are rounded; all other counts are exact.

E.2 Data-quality screening

Before final training, candidate rows were checked for exact and near duplicates across source and evaluation collections using question, passage, and option matching, shared eight-word sequences, and MinHash similarity (Broder, 1997). This removed 3,222 of 377,942 candidate rows. We did not replace them, leaving the 374,720-question final mixture reported in Table 2.
